articles.title: Tomato

sections.heading: Meet the crop
paragraphs: Tomatoes are warm-season fruiting plants. Leaves, stems and fruit offer different clues; the classifier compares leaves only.
Plant family: Solanaceae.

sections.heading: Growing thoughtfully
paragraphs: Give plants a sunny position and support them with a stake or cage.
Keep moisture reasonably consistent. Soil testing can guide fertility choices.

sections.heading: Reading leaf health
paragraphs: A healthy model match does not rule out an unsupported disease, pest, nutritional issue or stress. Observe the whole plant and its growing conditions.

articles.title: Maize
articles.summary: Long leaves. A closer look at the details.

sections.heading: Meet the crop
paragraphs: Maize has long, narrow leaves. Lesion shape and both leaf surfaces can help distinguish leaf problems; a photograph alone cannot confirm their cause.
Plant family: Poaceae.

sections.heading: Growing thoughtfully
paragraphs: Use locally adapted seed and soil-test recommendations.
For garden sweet corn, sow into warm soil and avoid drought stress. This source concerns sweet corn; field-maize schedules need local advice.

articles.title: Potato

sections.heading: Meet the crop
paragraphs: Ordinary potato is a nightshade crop grown from seed tubers. Sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) is a different, unsupported species. Roots and tubers are outside the leaf model’s scope.
Plant family: Solanaceae.

sections.heading: Growing thoughtfully
paragraphs: Start with disease-free seed tubers from a reputable certified supplier.
Choose a sunny site and hill soil around growing plants to cover developing tubers.

articles.title: Bell Pepper
articles.summary: Warmth, steady growth and watchful care.

sections.heading: Growing thoughtfully

Plant in warm conditions and use soil-test advice rather than guessing fertilizer rates.

articles.title: Cabbage
articles.summary: A tight head of layered leaves.

sections.heading: Meet the crop
paragraphs: Cabbage is a heading brassica suited to cooler growing conditions. It is available here for education; AgriVision has no trained cabbage classifier.
Plant family: Brassicaceae.

sections.heading: Growing thoughtfully
paragraphs: Use fertile, well-drained soil that retains moisture.
Plan rotation away from related brassica crops and maintain steady water supply. Local seasons differ from the source’s Minnesota calendar.

articles.title: Collard Greens
articles.summary: Broad leaves, grown for the table.

sections.heading: Meet the crop
paragraphs: Collards are a non-heading, leafy brassica. Their shared species with cabbage does not make crop images or trained disease classes interchangeable. AgriVision cannot diagnose collards.
Plant family: Brassicaceae.

sections.heading: Growing thoughtfully
paragraphs: Choose a sunny site with amended soil.
Use a soil test to guide nutrition. Suitability of planting dates and varieties depends on local climate.

articles.title: Early blight
articles.summary: A pattern worth checking, not a diagnosis.
symptoms: Older, lower leaves may develop dark brown spots with concentric rings and surrounding yellowing.
Similar spots can have other causes. Check stems, the spread of symptoms and weather history.

sections.heading: Context matters
paragraphs: Keep foliage dry, reduce soil splash and improve airflow. Resistance can reduce damage without providing complete protection.

sections.heading: Before acting
paragraphs: Confirm the crop and compare several leaves. A model match is an educational prompt, not a laboratory diagnosis or pesticide prescription.

articles.title: Late blight
symptoms: Large irregular brown blotches may have gray-green margins.
In damp conditions, pale growth may occur on affected tissues. Symptoms may spread rapidly.

sections.heading: Context matters
paragraphs: Late blight is caused by a water mold (oomycete). Suspected rapid spread deserves prompt local professional assessment; an app score cannot confirm it.

sections.heading: Before acting
paragraphs: Confirm the crop and compare several leaves. A model match is an educational prompt, not a laboratory diagnosis or pesticide prescription.

articles.title: Bacterial spot
symptoms: Tomato leaves may show small brown spots with yellow halos; centers can fall out.
Pepper leaf spots can look different, without the same halo or holes. Spots alone do not identify a bacterium.

sections.heading: Context matters
paragraphs: Use reputable seed or transplants, avoid wet handling and reduce splashing water. Symptoms can resemble other leaf-spot diseases.

sections.heading: Before acting

articles.title: Tomato leaf mold
symptoms: Pale yellow patches on the upper surface may align with olive-brown, velvety growth underneath.
Older leaves may be affected first; humidity and protected growing conditions provide useful context.

sections.heading: Context matters
paragraphs: Leaf mold is often associated with humid greenhouse or high-tunnel production. Good ventilation and keeping foliage dry are useful prevention principles.

sections.heading: Before acting

articles.title: Maize common rust
articles.summary: Look for raised pustules on both sides.
symptoms: Rust-colored to brown elongated pustules can occur on both leaf surfaces.
Other rusts and leaf diseases can resemble common rust in a photograph.

sections.heading: Context matters
paragraphs: Locally suitable resistant hybrids are an important preventive choice. Inspect both sides of the leaf and seek confirmation before treatment decisions.

articles.title: Maize gray leaf spot
articles.summary: Follow the veins, then consider the context.
symptoms: Mature gray-brown lesions often look rectangular, with parallel edges bounded by veins.
Lesion shape varies among hybrids and can resemble other maize leaf spots.

sections.heading: Context matters
paragraphs: Warm, humid conditions and infected crop debris can favor disease. Resistant hybrids and crop rotation are preventive options to discuss locally.

articles.title: Maize northern leaf blight
articles.summary: Long lesions are a clue, not proof.
symptoms: Elongated, canoe-shaped lesions may become tan and progress from lower leaves upward.
Some bacterial blights and other maize conditions can look similar.

sections.heading: Context matters
paragraphs: Resistance in locally suitable hybrids is a useful preventive choice. Assess disease development across plants, rather than relying on a single image.

articles.title: Black rot in brassicas
articles.summary: Educational reading for crops outside the model.
symptoms: Yellow V-shaped areas may begin at leaf margins, with darkened veins.
These clues are not unique enough for an app-based confirmation.

sections.heading: Reduce opportunities for spread
paragraphs: Black rot is bacterial and can spread in water. Use clean seed or transplants, avoid working in wet plants and consider rotation and residue management with local advice.

sections.heading: Scope matters
paragraphs: Both cabbage and collards are educational topics only. No brassica disease or healthy class has been added to the classifier.

articles.title: Who is chewing the leaves?
articles.scientific_name: Pieris rapae / Trichoplusia ni / Plutella xylostella
articles.summary: Look for the pest, not just its damage.
symptoms: Caterpillars may leave ragged holes or thin window-like patches between veins.
Inspect both leaf surfaces for larvae, eggs and droppings. Holes can have other causes.

sections.heading: A closer inspection
paragraphs: Cabbageworm, cabbage looper and diamondback moth larvae are examples described by the source. Local pest species and pressure may differ.

sections.heading: Gentle first steps
paragraphs: In small gardens, hand removal and appropriate row covers are physical management options. Check regularly and identify the insect before choosing a control.

sections.heading: AI limitation
paragraphs: AgriVision does not identify insects or classify pest damage, including on its four supported crops.

articles.title: A calmer growing routine
articles.scientific_name: Crop-specific observation; no universal disease label
articles.summary: Good habits begin before a photograph.
symptoms: Record where symptoms started and whether they are spreading.
Compare affected and unaffected leaves; check both surfaces.

sections.heading: Know what you planted
paragraphs: Record the crop and cultivar. Related plants are not interchangeable for diagnosis, planting dates or care.

sections.heading: Water and soil
paragraphs: Use soil testing to guide nutrition. For tomatoes, watering at the base and reducing soil splash can help keep foliage dry. Adjust water management to the crop and local conditions.

sections.heading: Use the guide thoughtfully
paragraphs: US extension references describe their own regional conditions. This library deliberately omits regional calendars, pesticide doses and claims of field accuracy. Ask a local agricultural adviser about urgent or uncertain problems.
